opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the phrase "liberal arts" is meant to evoke something quite specific. Historically, the liberal arts were the set of ways of thinking that a free person needed in order to participate in society: to reason, to argue, to understand the world they lived in. And I think if you ask what that set looks like today, it's changed. We live in a world where so many of the decisions that affect people's lives are being made through systems that collect data, make inferences, and then act on those inferences at scale. If you don't understand something about how that works, you're not really a full participant.

Now, why those three in particular? Computational thinking is about algorithms, about procedures, about what can be done efficiently and at scale. That's obviously central. Inferential thinking is statistics, really, in the broad sense: how do you reason under uncertainty, how do you go from data to conclusions, what's the error bar, what's the counterfactual, what would have happened otherwise. And people often forget that piece. They think if you have enough data and enough compute the uncertainty goes away, and it doesn't. It just moves around.

But the third piece, the economic piece, is the one I've been emphasizing more and more, because I think it's been largely missing from the conversation about AI. These systems are not just one agent sitting alone making predictions. They're embedded in collections of people and organizations that have their own goals, their own information, their own incentives. As soon as you have multiple decision-makers, you have strategic behavior, you have markets, you have mechanisms, you have questions of who benefits and who bears the cost. Economics has thought about those things for a long time, with concepts like incentive compatibility, contracts, and equilibrium, and those ideas need to be fused with the computational and inferential ones.

So my view is that the real engineering discipline that's emerging, and it is an engineering discipline, not just "intelligence" in some abstract sense, sits at the intersection of those three. Think of a recommendation system, a ride-sharing platform, a medical system deciding on treatments, or a financial market. In each case you need all three lenses at once. If you only bring one, you build something brittle, or unfair, or something that just doesn't serve the people it's meant to serve.

And I'd say this is also a corrective to the current narrative, which is very focused on building one superintelligent entity that imitates a human. I think that's the wrong goal, frankly. The more interesting and more useful goal is building systems, collectives really, that work well for humans, that create markets and connections and value, much the way the economy itself is a kind of intelligent system without any single brain in charge. To think about that properly, a well-educated person, not just a specialist, needs some fluency in all three modes of thought. That's why I call it the liberal arts of our era.

r001.rationale: It defines computational thinking in terms of algorithms, procedures, efficiency, and scale, but does not say this reasoning extends beyond computers to other disciplines.

r002.rationale: It discusses inferential reasoning under uncertainty, but does not explain that this reasoning can generate algorithms beyond computer science design principles.

r003.rationale: It explains how incentives and strategic behavior matter in AI systems, but does not connect incentive analysis specifically to language models or explain what context it adds beyond computational algorithms.

r004.rationale: It mentions uncertainty, error bars, and counterfactuals, but does not identify controlling data as a way statistical thinking helps prevent errors.

r005.rationale: It presents the three modes of thought as important for a well-educated person and an emerging engineering discipline, but does not propose them as an organizing framework for academia.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think if you go back and ask what the liberal arts were supposed to do, they were the set of ideas that a free person needed in order to participate in society, to reason about the world and about other people. In the medieval version that was grammar, logic, rhetoric, and then arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy. Those were the tools for thinking. And I'd argue that the tools for thinking in our era are these three things: computation, inference, and economics, and crucially the blend of them, not any one alone.

Computational thinking is about what can be done with finite resources, how you decompose a problem, what's an algorithm, what scales and what doesn't. Inferential thinking is about uncertainty, about what you can and can't conclude from data, about how wrong you might be and how to quantify that. And economic thinking is about the fact that there are other agents out there with their own goals, their own information, their own incentives, and that scarcity and interaction shape outcomes. Most of the real problems we care about, in healthcare, in transportation, in markets, in science, sit right at the intersection of those three. You have lots of data, you're uncertain, there are computational constraints, and there are people in the loop who will respond to whatever system you build.

The reason I use the phrase "liberal arts" rather than, say, "the new STEM," is that I don't think these are just technical specialties for engineers. If you're going to be a citizen in a world where decisions are increasingly mediated by data-driven systems, you need some literacy in all three. You need to understand why a prediction might be biased, why a recommendation system might be gaming you, why an aggregate statistic doesn't tell you what will happen to you as an individual. That's not a job skill, that's a way of being an educated person.

And frankly, I think the current framing around "AI" obscures this. The narrative is that we're building a single intelligent entity that will solve problems for us. I think the far more important and realistic picture is that we're building collective systems, markets and networks of people and algorithms, where value emerges from the interactions. To design those well, and to live well inside them, you need the inferential piece so you're honest about uncertainty, the computational piece so things actually run, and the economic piece so the incentives make the whole thing work for the people in it rather than against them. Bring those together and you have, I think, the intellectual core that a university ought to be teaching everyone, not just the computer science majors.

r001.rationale: It presents computational thinking as a general tool for reasoning about problems across fields such as healthcare, transportation, markets, and science, not just as a technical specialty.

r002.rationale: It describes inferential thinking as reasoning about uncertainty, but does not say that it generates algorithms beyond computer science design principles.

r003.rationale: It discusses incentives in collective systems involving people and algorithms, but does not specifically explain how incentive analysis supplies context around language models beyond what computational algorithms provide.

r004.rationale: It mentions biased predictions and limits of aggregate statistics, but does not identify controlling data as a means of preventing errors.

r005.rationale: It calls the combination of computational, inferential, and economic thinking the intellectual core a university should teach everyone.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think of the liberal arts as the things you need to learn to participate thoughtfully in the world, whatever profession you eventually pursue. And increasingly, that means understanding computation, uncertainty, and the ways people interact through systems.

Computational thinking lets you ask: How would I actually carry out this idea? What resources would it require? How does it behave as it grows? Inferential thinking asks: What can I learn from the data I have? What am I uncertain about? Does the evidence support the decision I’m about to make? Those are different questions. Having a lot of computation doesn’t make an inference valid.

And then economic thinking brings in the fact that there are other people involved. They have their own information, preferences, and incentives. When you build a system that recommends something or allocates a resource, you’re changing the environment in which those people act. Their responses change the data you’ll see next. So you can’t really separate the algorithm from the human system it’s embedded in.

That combination is useful far beyond someone who’s going to build machine learning systems. A doctor, a journalist, a policymaker, or a citizen needs ways to reason about evidence and about the consequences of decisions mediated by technology. I don’t mean that everyone needs to become a programmer or an economist. I mean these should become part of our shared intellectual toolkit, alongside the humanities: ways to ask better questions about the world we’re creating.

r001.rationale: It presents computational thinking as part of a shared intellectual toolkit useful to doctors, journalists, policymakers, and citizens, beyond people building machine learning systems.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty and evidence, but does not say that inferential uncertainty can generate algorithms beyond computer science design principles.

r003.rationale: It explains how incentives shape human systems around algorithms, but does not connect that point to language models.

r004.rationale: It mentions data and evidence, but does not identify controlling data as a way statistical thinking prevents errors.

r005.rationale: It calls the combination a shared intellectual toolkit and part of the liberal arts, but does not propose it as an organizing framework for academia.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, by liberal arts I mean a set of ways of thinking that allows you to engage with the world, whatever profession you eventually choose. And increasingly, the world we’re engaging with involves data, computation, and decisions that affect other people.

Computational thinking gives you a way to think about processes: how you represent a problem, how you break it into pieces, and what resources it takes to solve it. Inferential thinking asks how you learn something from limited observations. What does the data actually tell you? What uncertainty remains? What happens when the setting changes?

Economic thinking brings in the fact that you’re usually not making decisions in isolation. There are other people with their own information, preferences, and incentives. Your decision changes their situation, and their decisions change yours. So you have to think about how those interactions are organized.

These perspectives really need each other. You can build a computational system that makes good predictions and still produces a poor outcome because you haven’t thought about the incentives it creates. Or you can propose a desirable economic arrangement without asking whether people have enough information to participate, or whether it can actually be computed at the relevant scale.

So I wouldn’t want these subjects reserved for specialists. I’d want someone studying biology, or journalism, or public policy to have enough familiarity with all three to ask good questions. That’s the liberal arts role: giving people intellectual tools for understanding and participating in the world around them.

r001.rationale: It presents computational thinking as a general way to reason about problems and says people in fields such as biology, journalism, and public policy should learn it.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from limited observations and uncertainty, but does not explain that this reasoning can generate algorithms beyond computer science design principles.

r003.rationale: It explains how incentives affect outcomes, but does not connect incentive analysis to language models or contrast it with computational algorithms.

r004.rationale: It does not identify controlling data as a way statistical thinking prevents errors.

r005.rationale: It advocates teaching the three perspectives broadly as liberal arts, but does not propose them as an organizing framework for academia.
